description: We are team SailorMoon. We have experience in research, CS, AI, and more.
summary:
Testing hardware on Earth before it flies is much cheaper than finding out on the Moon that it doesn't work. But the field sites NASA tests at are often picked through experience and habit, and a place that's great for testing rover wheels might be useless for testing solar panels.

We built Analog Atlas to help with that choice. You pick a subsystem, like rover wheels, spacesuit boots or a lander's hazard cameras, and a target such as the lunar south pole or Jezero Crater. The Atlas then searches nearly 79,000 places on Earth and ranks the ones that match the conditions that subsystem will actually face. It uses NASA data like MODIS, MERRA-2, LOLA and MOLA. A second model compares terrain more closely around specific sites.

We checked our limits against the places NASA has really tested, from Black Point Lava Flow to the Atacama Desert. Every number shows where it came from, and anything we're unsure about is clearly marked. The goal is to help teams find better test sites faster, and to see what Earth can't simulate before they commit to a field campaign.
details:
Before anything goes to the Moon or Mars, NASA tests it on Earth, and we kept running into the same problem: no place on Earth is a perfect stand-in, so the real question is which place is good enough for the part you're testing. Analog Atlas answers that. You pick what you're testing (rover wheels, landing-hazard sensors, batteries in the cold) and where it's going (the lunar south pole or Jezero crater on Mars), and it ranks places on Earth for that one test, tells you what each place can and can't reproduce, and shows you how much to trust the answer.

Under the hood it works like a funnel. The website first screens 78,993 land squares of 55 km using open NASA and ESA data (LOLA, Diviner, MOLA, MODIS, MERRA-2, Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover), and pass/fail limits remove anywhere snow, plants or rain would spoil the test. A close-up check then re-measures the top 25 at 2 km, because a mountain range can look gentle from 55 km away.

Finally, our weighted nearest-neighbour model compares 100–200 candidate sites with real Moon and Mars terrain at matched scales. It is unsupervised, because there are only a handful of known NASA sites to learn from, and its weights come from published rover limits such as VIPER's 15° slope limit. The payoff is that test teams can look beyond the few sites NASA already uses, spend field-test money where it counts, and learn early which conditions (gravity, vacuum, the lunar day–night swing) belong in a lab or chamber instead.

The part we're proudest of is that we made honesty a feature. We hid NASA's own field sites from the model to see whether it would find them anyway. For lunar landing hazards it did: those sites beat 97% of alternatives, something random picks manage only 3 times in 10,000. Where the results were weaker, as with the rovers, where NASA also picks sites for road access, we show that openly instead of tuning it away. Every limit cites its source, and missing data never counts as a pass.

We built it in Python (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, rasterio, pytest) and a React + Vite web app with MapLibre, Three.js and Cesium, deployed on Vercel, with Claude as a coding assistant. Along the way we kept weighing scientific defensibility, comparing Earth and other worlds at the same scale, data licensing, validation against NASA's real test sites, and keeping it all understandable for people who aren't planetary scientists.
